hints: Look at the size of the rings in each pair. Sucrose is special because it is made from two different types of monosaccharide with different ring sizes.
Remember sucrose = alpha-glucose + fructose. Check for one 6-sided ring with the C1 OH pointing down, plus one 5-sided ring.
walkthrough:
**Recall what sucrose is made from**

Sucrose is a disaccharide made by condensation of two different hexoses.

Remember it simply as:
$$ \text{sucrose} = \alpha\text{-glucose} + \text{fructose} $$

**Use ring size to find fructose**

Glucose forms a 6-membered pyranose ring. Fructose forms a 5-membered furanose ring.

So first, eliminate any option with two 6-membered rings. That leaves only C and D, both have one 6-ring on the left and one 5-ring on the right.

**Check alpha-glucose versus beta-glucose**

Look at carbon 1 of the glucose (right side of the left ring). In alpha-glucose the OH on C1 points down, on the opposite side to the CH2OH group. In beta-glucose it points up, on the same side.

In C, the left ring has H up and OH down at C1, so it is alpha-glucose. In D, it has OH up and H down, so it is beta-glucose. Only C gives alpha-glucose + fructose, which is sucrose.

options.A: Both molecules are 6-membered hexose rings, so there is no 5-membered fructose present. This cannot be sucrose.
options.B: Both molecules are 6-membered alpha-glucose rings. Two alpha-glucose units would form maltose, not sucrose.
options.C: Left is 6-membered alpha-glucose and right is 5-membered fructose. This is the correct pair to form sucrose by condensation.
options.D: Right is fructose but left is beta-glucose, with the C1 OH pointing up. Sucrose requires alpha-glucose, so this is incorrect.
